cosmo_chart_title: Three distance measures in an expanding universe
cosmo_epochs_title: The same comoving galaxy at two cosmic times
cosmo_intro: Redshift tells us how much space grew while light traveled. Compare how long the journey took with the galaxy’s separation then and today. Distances and ages are inferred from the chosen expansion model.
cosmo_control_help: Drag the slider or chart. Arrow keys change z by 0.1; Shift changes it by 1. Home selects 0 and End selects 15. Both views and the readouts use the same redshift.
cosmo_inferred_note: The distance and age remain model calculations.
cosmo_chosen_z: Chosen redshift. Import a published galaxy example from the spectrum lab above to use its measured redshift.
cosmo_chart_caption: Vertical scale: billions of light-years (Gly). The light-travel equivalent is c × travel time. It differs from the galaxy’s separation because space expanded during the journey.
cosmo_epochs_caption: White cross: observer. Oval: a galaxy following cosmic expansion. Both rows use the same 0–50 Gly scale. Galaxy symbols have fixed illustrative sizes. These are separations at two times, not a photon’s path.
cosmo_today_age_metric: Universe age today in this model
cosmo_zero_status: At z = 0 these expansion distances are zero. This is the limit at the observer, not a statement that every zero-redshift object is nearby. Local motions can cancel cosmological redshift.

cosmo_peak_note: The dashed curve turns down at high z: the universe was much smaller when that light left. This does not make the galaxy closer today.
cosmo_planck_status: Rounded Planck 2018 inputs: H₀ = 67.4 km/s/Mpc; matter fraction Ωₘ = 0.315. This explorer uses a flat matter + Λ approximation.
cosmo_h0_scope: Only H₀ changes here. The matter fraction remains 0.315; this is a controlled comparison, not a new cosmological fit.
cosmo_h0_help: A larger H₀ gives shorter inferred distances and ages at the same redshift when the matter fraction stays fixed. Each Mpc is about 3.26 million light-years; H₀ is an expansion rate, not a speed for every galaxy.
cosmo_measurement_scope: Planck Collaboration (2018 results, published 2020) infers H₀ = 67.4 ± 0.5 km/s/Mpc and Ωₘ = 0.315 ± 0.007 under base ΛCDM. Riess et al. (2022) measure H₀ = 73.04 ± 1.04 km/s/Mpc with the Cepheid–supernova distance ladder. These are named studies, not a live consensus estimate. Quoted uncertainties are not propagated into these curves.
cosmo_limits: The model assumes a homogeneous, spatially flat universe with matter and a constant Λ. It omits radiation, detailed neutrino evolution, peculiar velocities and gravitational redshifts. The range ends at z = 15; it does not model recombination, the CMB or inflation. Redshift alone does not give a model-independent distance.
cosmo_equations: a = 1/(1+z). E(z) = √[Ωₘ(1+z)³ + 1−Ωₘ]. Separation today: D = (c/H₀) ∫₀ᶻ dz′/E(z′). Separation then: D/(1+z), equal to angular-diameter distance in this flat model. Travel time: ∫₀ᶻ dz′/[(1+z′)H₀E(z′)]. The age uses the exact matter + Λ solution. Distances on the chart share one linear scale.
two_independent_ways_to_measure_the_cu: Two published routes to the current expansion rate give different results. Planck 2018 CMB data interpreted with base ΛCDM imply H₀ = 67.4 ± 0.5 km/s/Mpc. The SH0ES Cepheid–supernova distance ladder gives 73.04 ± 1.04 km/s/Mpc (Riess et al., 2022). JWST observations test specific crowding and photometry errors in Cepheids; they do not rule out every distance-ladder systematic. The cause of the disagreement remains unresolved. Different distance indicators and cosmological assumptions need careful comparison.
